concepts.title: Prediction bias
concepts.outcome: Compute prediction bias as a quick health check on a classifier, and list what can cause it.

keyPoints.text: Calculating prediction bias, the difference between the mean of a model's predictions and the mean of the ground-truth labels, is a quick check that can flag problems with the model or training data early.

anchor.start: Calculating prediction bias is a quick

keyPoints.text: A model trained on data where 5% of emails are spam should predict, on average, that 5% are spam; then it has zero prediction bias, though it might still have other problems.

anchor.start: A model trained on a dataset

keyPoints.text: If that model instead predicts spam 50% of the time, something is wrong with the training data, the new data it is applied to, or the model itself; any significant gap between the two means suggests prediction bias.

anchor.start: If the model instead predicts 50%
anchor.end: the model has some prediction bias

keyPoints.text: Prediction bias can come from biased or noisy data, including biased sampling of the training set; regularisation so strong it oversimplifies the model; bugs in the training pipeline; or features insufficient for the task.

misconceptions.claim: A model with zero prediction bias is a good model.
misconceptions.correction: Zero prediction bias only means the average prediction matches the average label, as when a model predicts 5% spam on data that is 5% spam; the model might still have other problems.

An odds ratio compares two odds, and coefficients live on the log-odds scale.
Why a coefficient is not a fixed change in probability rests on the S-shape of the sigmoid.
Log loss is motivated by the sigmoid's non-constant rate of change.
Regularisation is the second of the two training differences, after log loss, and is about loss being driven towards 0.
A decision is taken on the probability the sigmoid produces.
A threshold is the simplest decision rule on a predicted probability.
The confusion matrix counts the outcomes of labels made at a threshold.
Watching the threshold move the counts needs the four counts first.
The counts move as the threshold moves.
Accuracy is computed from all four cells of the confusion matrix.
Recall is computed from true positives and false negatives.
The false positive rate is computed from false positives and true negatives.
Precision is computed from true and false positives.
Balanced accuracy fixes the way plain accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.
Balanced accuracy is the average recall per class.
The trade-off is between precision and recall.
The trade-off is between precision and recall.
The trade-off comes from how the threshold moves false positives and false negatives.
F1 combines precision and recall.
F1 combines precision and recall.
Choosing a metric means choosing a side of the trade-off.
The false positive rate is one of the metrics to choose between.
An ROC curve plots the true positive rate.
An ROC curve plots against the false positive rate.
An ROC curve traces the rates as the threshold moves.
AUC is the area under the ROC curve.
Precision-recall curves are introduced as the alternative to ROC and AUC on imbalanced data.
A precision-recall curve draws the trade-off across thresholds.
The case for a precision-recall curve rests on class imbalance.
A cost-based threshold applies the reasoning used to choose a metric.

Tuning leaves the ROC and precision-recall curves unchanged, which needs both curves.
Calibration asks whether the predicted probability can be read as it is.

Whether calibration changes AUC needs AUC first.
What a Brier score says about calibration needs calibration first.
Log loss as a metric builds on log loss as a training loss.
Prediction bias compares the average predicted probability with the average label.
Too-strong regularisation is one cause of prediction bias.
